name: Spiti Bhoti
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Sharma, Suhnu R. 1979. Phonological structure of Spiti; D.D. Sharma 1992 'Spitian' grammar sketch (per Glottolog MED list); neither found online

new_statements.quote: Three tones, three pitch-levels of intonational phonemes, three terminal contours, three junctures, and nazalization are found among suprasegmentals. [p. 83] ... A three term tonal system, falling, level and rising tone is found in Spiti and associated with the word or lexical item. A given lexical item may be assigned to one or the other supra-segmental category and termed as a Tone 1 word, a Tone 2 word, or a Tone 3 word [p. 104]
new_statements.citation: Sharma, Suhnu R. 1979. Phonological structure of Spiti. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 4(2): 83-110.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Spiti is described as a lexical tone language: every word belongs to one of three tone classes (Tone 1 falling, Tone 2 level, Tone 3 rising), with phrase-level intonation contours and junctures on top. The suprasegmental inventory is enumerated exhaustively and stress/accent is not among its members; no source examined states a stress position. The later LSI Bhotia sketch (three tones + nasalization), Hein 2017 (register tone) and Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 (two-way high/low pitch tone for the W section incl. Spiti) agree that the word-level prosodic contrast is tonal.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Sharma 1979 notes falling-tone syllables are longer than level/rising ones (p. 105); LSI 2023 notes falling tone does not occur word-initially (p. 1034); Mehta 2021 found only five tone-bearing words in her Pin-valley data (p. 112).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/lexical-item level tone assignment (Sharma 1979 p. 104: 'associated with the word or lexical item'); intonational pitch levels and terminal contours are utterance-level (pp. 107-110). Sharma's data: Spiti valley fieldwork 1972-73, 'the whole valley'.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 1979 describes 'Spiti (locally Piti)' from valley-wide fieldwork 1972-73 = spit1240. Hein 2001/2017 describe the Tabo village variety (Tabo Tibetan, 'as identical to Spiti Tibetan' per Hein 2017: 113) = spit1240. The LSI 2023 'Bhotia' chapter is Himachal Bhotia recorded in Spiti with informants also from Kullu/Manali (winter migrants) = Spiti Bhoti, possibly with Lahaul (Stod Bhoti, stod1241) admixture. Mehta 2021's consultant is from Sangnam, Pin valley (Spiti). Tournadre & Suzuki 2023 treat Spiti with Garzha and Khunu-Töt as the Western section.

sources.quote: Three tones, three pitch-levels of intonational phonemes, three terminal contours, three junctures, and nazalization are found among suprasegmentals. [p. 83] ... A three term tonal system, falling, level and rising tone is found in Spiti and associated with the word or lexical item. A given lexical item may be assigned to one or the other supra-segmental category and termed as a Tone 1 word, a Tone 2 word, or a Tone 3 word [p. 104]
sources.note: Whole article is the phonology. Suprasegmentals enumerated as three tones (falling/level/rising, lexically assigned per word), three intonational pitch levels, three terminal contours, three junctures and nasalization (p. 83, pp. 104-110). The word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the 28 scanned pages; no stress or accent placement is described.

sources.citation: Sharma, D. D. 1989. Tribal Languages of Himachal Pradesh, Part I (Studies in Tibeto-Himalayan Languages II). Delhi: Mittal.
sources.note: Covers Lahauli (Pattani etc.) only; preface announces 'Part II. Tibeto-Himalayan Dialects of Spiti, Kinnaur...'. Not about Spiti; checked only to confirm the Spitian sketch is in Part II (1992), which was not found online.

sources.citation: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India. 2023 (fieldwork 1995-2008; Bhotia chapter by S. Ganesh Baskaran, data collected in Spiti July-Aug 2009). Linguistic Survey of India: Himachal Pradesh. Chapter 5, 'Bhotia' (vol. pp. ~1015-1090).
sources.note: §2 Phonology: 'The supra-segmentals are divided into two sub-types that is tone and nasalization' (p. 1017); §2.6 Suprasegmental phonemes: three contrastive tones (level, rising, falling), 'every vowel possesses any one of the above mentioned three tones', falling tone does not occur word-initially (pp. 1033-1034). No mention of stress in the Bhotia chapter.

sources.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: An introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan. Paris: LACITO Publications. Part 2 (chs. 7 and 9).
sources.note: Ch. 7.3: pitch tone 'attested mainly in Ü, Tsang, Tö, Spiti, Ladakh Jangthang...' (p. 236); 7.3.3 Stress: 'The distinction of stress is attested mainly in Balti' (p. 242); 7.3.4: prosody of Spiti and Balti influenced by Hindi/Urdu (p. 243). Ch. 9.9.6 (p. 604): W-section dialects incl. Spiti 'have a pitch tone system generally with a two-way contrast (high and low)'. No statement of stress placement for Spiti; secondary survey.

sources.note: Segmental inventory only; 'Sharma (1981) discusses the presence of three tones in Spiti namely level, rising and falling. Within the data collected for the present study, only five words were found to exhibit tone' (p. 112). No mention of stress. Cites D.D. Sharma 1992 'Spitian' (pp. 57, 61, 62) for verb morphology.
